**Follow-up length carries information.** A machine still working after two days and one still working after two years are both “not failed,” but they provide very different evidence about lifetime. Binary classification can lose that distinction if both are labeled as permanent negatives. [1](https://probml.github.io/pml-book/book1.html)

Right censoring means the event time exceeds the last observed follow-up, not that the event will never happen. Survival analysis includes that partial information. Kaplan–Meier estimates the fraction surviving beyond each time while adjusting the at-risk set. Cox models relative hazard through covariates and a baseline hazard.

**Hazard is an instantaneous event rate among those still at risk, not a cumulative probability.** A Cox multiplier of two means twice the modeled hazard under its proportional-hazards assumptions, not necessarily twice the probability of failure by every horizon.

Check censoring assumptions, changing effects over time, and competing events. Evaluate survival probabilities at useful horizons and inspect calibration, not only ranking. Survival methods are valuable when event timing and censoring matter; they are not automatically superior if the application truly has complete labels for one fixed horizon.

**Technical details and references.**

Survival analysis models time to an event while accounting for observations whose event has not happened by the last follow-up. Kaplan–Meier estimates the survival curve; Cox models a baseline hazard multiplied by covariate-dependent relative risk. [1](https://probml.github.io/pml-book/book1.html)

$$h(t\mid x)=h_0(t)e^{\beta^Tx}.$$

Treating censored cases as permanent negatives in binary classification loses follow-up information and biases labels. Survival methods require assumptions such as appropriate independent censoring, and Cox requires proportional hazards for its standard interpretation. Competing events and recurrent failures need extensions. Evaluate time-specific calibration and discrimination at clinically/operationally relevant horizons, not only one aggregate concordance score.
